_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Working Lands & Industry' — forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture, the resource economy that defines the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: geopolitical and war news with no resource-economy connection; consumer tech and gadget reviews; wildlife content with no agricultural or working-lands relevance; crime and judicial news unrelated to resource industries; financial market and stock ticker stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Trade-press journalism counts fully: equipment, markets, and operations coverage is a real fit, not a near-zero. A BC tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent working-lands journalism. BC/Cariboo forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture stories land here (mill closures, beetle kill, BCTS, Cariboo ranchers and water rights, local mine operations, Cariboo Cattlemen) — and so does outstanding national trade reporting with real operational or economic depth.
- 55-79: Solid resource-economy journalism anywhere in Canada or beyond — Western Producer or Northern Miner-style coverage of farm machinery, harvest technology, livestock and commodity markets, mining operations and exploration, AgTech and precision agriculture, silviculture, sawmills, drone survey work, mine automation, and labour/workforce stories in these industries. Most genuine trade journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Broader agriculture, forestry, or mining news with clear working-lands relevance but thin reporting — general farm economics, international resource-industry briefs, climate impacts on working lands.
- 15-29: Tangential mentions — a business, policy, or science story that touches forestry/agriculture/mining in passing, or Cariboo civic news unrelated to working lands.

ANCHORS: 'Williams Lake sawmill cuts second shift as beetle-kill supply dwindles' → 95. 'New John Deere baler cuts hay-drying time by a third' → 70. 'Cattle futures slip on weaker export demand' → 60. 'Global copper prices hit two-year high' → 40.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Nieman Storyboard] Journalist Wudan Yan on the importance of fact-checking as ‘peer review’
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Fact-checking in journalism can mean many different things — and the process can vary whether you're working on a book or podcast, a longform magazine feature, or a breaking story in a 24/7 newsroom. 

But given the rise of disinformation and AI content, we need fact-checking more than ever. And there's an opportunity to bring more clarity to the process, both for journalists and for our audiences.  

This week's guest on the Nieman Storyboard podcast, journalist Wudan Yan, is founder of the fact-checking agency Factual, which provides fact-checking services for journalists, authors, and nonprofits. Writing for her newsletter, she recently made the case that fact-checking itself needs to evolve to meet the moment, so we talked about how journalists can make the most of the process in their own work.


[ Follow us in Apple Podcasts, Spotify, or your favorite podcast app. ]

“ My true fear is that people are just going to become desensitized to the amount of fake information that's out there and not care,” Yan told me. But “as long as people care and value accuracy, I think fact-checking has a place, I think journalism has a place.” 

Yan was pursuing a doctoral degree in cancer biology when she decided to make the jump into journalism, starting as a fact-checker for publications including the science magazine Nautilus. She eventually moved into reporting, developing an understanding for what it meant to tell science and environmental stories through a narrative lens. Her writing has appeared in The Atlantic, California Sunday Magazine, High Country News, MIT Technology Review, The New York Times, and Popular Mechanics, among other publications. 

The excerpts below are edited for length and clarity.

Defining fact-checking as a form of ‘peer review’

I think people value accuracy intellectually. … Humans who conduct fact-checking are expensive. We're not AI, and so there's a price to pay, and it's really important for me to work with clients who understand that value.

 I usually describe fact-checking as a peer review for accuracy in the same way that coming from my previous career as a scientist, you cannot peer review your own work in a journal for publication. Somebody else has to do that peer reviewing for you. So when you are writing for a daily newspaper, if you're just making sure that what you wrote that's about to go to press is accurate, you're double-checking yourself. You're not fact-checking yourself.

On organizing your reporting and taking time to process it

Early in my career, I got a really amazing glimpse into how other reporters organize their work, and that gave me frameworks for how to organize my own reporting. So I use Google Drive, and for a project like this turmeric feature [“The Vice of Spice: Confronting Lead-Tainted Turmeric"], that's the main folder. There are interview notes, audio files, research papers, and then another folder just called field reporting. Quickly, you're going to realize all I have in my life are these like Russian nesting dolls of Google Drive folders.

Then outside of Google Drive — I think this is an Ira Glass tactic — once you're done with all the interviews and field reporting from a day, you kind of just sit and basically journal about the day.

The way that I interpreted that advice was to write about my day as if what I discovered that day was going to be the lead of my story. So I did that every single day, even if there wasn't really a story and it was really boring. It just got me into a very cinematic way of writing.

Quite honestly, in many of the features that I have produced over my career, I am just plagiarizing off of myself when I start writing the lead. And I can't tell you how many hours it saves me there because I've already done that hard work.

On the future of fact-checking and journalism

 I think for fact-checking right now, I don't think the robots are going to come for this type of work yet. I went to a professional conference the other weekend, and just talking to people who are getting all these spammy emails from AI agents being like, "If you want us to verify a paper, send it to us, and it's $25, and we'll look at primary sources only and let you know how a claim stacks up." And nobody in my world is really taking that seriously. I'm curious about who's paying $25 for a robot to check a claim, or what's attributed to a single paper. AI can make a recommendation, but you still definitely need a human to make sure that whatever's coming up on Google search or Claude or ChatGPT actually makes sense for the context and the story that's involved. 

 My true fear is that people are just going to become desensitized to the amount of fake information that's out there and not care. … As long as people care and value accuracy, I think fact-checking has a place, I think journalism has a place.

  • Wudan Yan's website

  • Factual agency 

  • Nautilus Magazine 

  • “The Vice of Spice: Confronting Lead-Tainted Turmeric" (Wudan Yan, Undark, 2023)

  • UC Berkeley Journalism Fellowships

  • “We need fact-checkers more than ever. Here's how to work with one.” (Kim Cross, Nieman Storyboard 2025)

items.title: [Fast Company] What to think about before making a big ask from your direct reports
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

As a supervisor, you have some ability to dictate what your direct reports work on. The requests you make should typically fit their job description, though most descriptions have a catchall “other duties as assigned” attached, which is likely to cover you.

That said, the jobs you give someone generally have a particular expectation of the skills required, the hours to be worked, and the stress level associated with the tasks. If you’re going to ask someone to do something that far exceeds the norm, there are a few things you should consider first.

Are you taking advantage?

The people you supervise probably want to keep you happy. You have power over their evaluations, and your recommendation can help to propel them to a promotion or other opportunities. This means that when you ask your reports to do something, they are likely to agree.

You should make sure that when you’re making a big ask, the employee is likely to benefit rather than suffer from doing the work. For example, you have work that needs to be done, but you don’t want to put the time of a higher-priced employee onto it. If you’re going to try to save money by using a less-experienced person, you should be careful that you’re not adding a lot of extra hours or stress to their work just to cut costs.

Your reports pay attention to the hours that other people are putting in. If you ask far greater effort of them than you put in yourself, that can rankle in ways that may ultimately cause dedicated people to want to work elsewhere.

What are the long-term benefits?

When you are going to make that big ask, think about what benefits that work is likely to have for your direct report. Talk to them about those benefits when you make the request.

For example, a big project may give a newer employee a chance to work with senior leaders, or do work that is visible to them. That can help bring them future opportunities. A significant project may also help them to expand their capacities by taking on new experiences. That project may also lead to overtime (depending on how they are paid), allowing them to take home more money.

One reason for thinking through the benefits of this additional work for an employee is that you may discover that the assignment might be more beneficial for another member of your team. The more you can use significant tasks to develop your team, the easier it is to ask them to go beyond the norm.

What will sweeten the deal?

Of course, there are also some pretty onerous tasks that someone has to take on—and you may decide that burden should fall on one of your team members. In this situation, consider whether there are ways to make the burden less significant.

If the job is going to require additional travel or a lot of extra hours, you might want to offer compensatory time off or some time with a flexible work arrangement to reward them for taking one for the team.

If you’re going to give a team member a significant responsibility that adds effort and stress to their work, consider ways to help use that to further their career. Give that person additional mentorship to accelerate their career path or provide them with chances to engage with senior leaders who might ultimately be able to find additional opportunities for them.

When you use big asks as a way to give flexibility or career benefit to your team members, you create trust. The members of your team will talk to each other, and you don’t want to get the reputation of someone who drives people hard without looking out for them. When you give people challenge as well as support, you provide a motivating environment that allows the team to excel, even under difficult circumstances.
